38	## Architecture
39	
40	The executable path is deliberately shallow:
41	
42	```text
43	cmd/dev/main.go
44	  -> cli.Execute()
45	  -> cli.NewRootCommandWithIO()
46	  -> App.Load()
47	  -> Cobra command handler
48	  -> domain package(s)
49	```
50	
51	`internal/cli` assembles commands, parses flags, invokes services, and renders output. Keep policy out of command handlers; it belongs in independently testable domain packages:
52	
53	- `config` owns defaults, TOML overlays, validation, and XDG paths.
54	- `gitx` is the Git porcelain boundary and canonicalizes repository identity through the shared Git common directory.
55	- `submodule` owns versioned workspace-member intent and reversible child-clone disposal mechanisms. `gitx` supplies the local gitlink graph; `taskflow` owns recursive lifecycle policy and fresh remote-proof ordering. Gitlink checkouts are legitimate submodules, not nested managed linked worktrees.
56	- `task` persists only human intent Git cannot derive: task mode/state, owner, next action, and runtime hints. Lifecycle callers use exact-record revisions and locked compare-and-update/delete transactions rather than treating a previously read task as current.
57	- `wt` owns managed linked-worktree creation, placement, provisioning plans, and safe removal. Runtimes never create or manage Git worktrees; they surface checkout or experiment paths selected and validated by the calling `dev` flow, including managed, external, or adopted worktrees and non-Git Try directories.
58	- `runtime` abstracts Herdr, tmux, Zellij, and the no-multiplexer backend. Handles are backend-qualified hints and must be checked against live checkout coverage before reuse.
59	- `taskflow` is the UI-agnostic lifecycle authority: it separates recorded intent, typed live observations, immutable guarded plans, approvals, and partial result ledgers. Apply locks and reloads task/Git/worktree/runtime/artifact/remote identity, then rejects stale authority before mutation.
60	- `repo` discovers and deduplicates repositories; `inventory` joins repositories, Git state, tasks, all registered worktrees, and live runtime data. CLI listings and UI projections consume this joined view.
61	- `agentinterop` owns explicit MCP/skill/instruction transfer plans, guarded apply, stanza/link ownership, private recovery, and optional recipes. Native agent files and skills locks remain authoritative; only explicit preparation/check/launch paths may execute a provider or MCP server. Recovery belongs outside Git, credentials remain runtime references, and native Windows writes fail closed pending verified ACL/identity support.
62	- `triage` owns read-only cross-repository findings, clone-bound local intent, ignored-directory policy and reviewed batch ledgers; `triagetui` is its independent UI. Synchronization uses taskflow plans, and protected cleanup adds guards inside the existing repository lock and immediately before removal. Local scans never reconcile Try catalog entries.
63	- `flowtui` is an independent Bubble Tea model for the preview `dev flow` repository state-machine UI. It receives repository reads and taskflow Plan/Apply callbacks; do not embed it in or add a mode to the dashboard's `tui` model.
64	- `catalog` stores stable repository/Try identity and personal metadata. `experiment` owns Try creation, archive/restore, and graduation, including intent records and rollback/reconciliation around moves.
65	- `note` stores multiple repository thoughts as durable Markdown keyed by catalog ID and maintains a rebuildable SQLite FTS index. It is distinct from task context and the catalog's single metadata summary.
66	- `tui` owns Bubble Tea state/rendering only. `internal/cli/tui.go` injects callbacks to the same services used by non-interactive commands.
67	- `stats` is durable SQLite data; `diskusage`, note FTS, and forge/gitignore data are regenerable caches. Do not treat stats as cache.
68	- `agenthistory` owns explicit transcript/file retention policy, immutable source-bound archive copies, Git lookup/sync and isolated history migration. Archive bindings/recovery stay in private state, ordinary status never contacts remotes, and source writers/index bytes remain untouched by archiving. `artifact` keeps old commit handoffs and adds externally verified archive receipts; taskflow includes ignored capture readiness in its guarded authority.
69	- `hygiene` owns configurable secret/privacy policy, index/worktree/frozen-history scans, private identity rules and signed replacement plans. Raw findings/recovery stay outside Git; hook setup preserves foreign hooks. Large text transactions explicitly opt into configedit’s Windows backend; existing configuration flows retain their platform contracts.
70	- `feedback` owns durable private reports, sanitized public drafts, revision-bound issue/comment publication receipts and exact repair plans. CLI adapts its repair backend to the shared start flow; agent launch is explicit and prompt context never becomes a public issue body.
71	- `forge` wraps optional `gh`, `glab`, and Azure CLI integrations and must degrade to local Git behavior when they are unavailable.
72	- `sshhost` owns bounded static discovery of the active user OpenSSH Include closure, canonical files under `~/.ssh/dev.d`, public-key selection/generation/bootstrap, fresh authentication proofs, and the explicit handoff into dev fleet. OpenSSH and plain `ssh -G` remain semantic authority; ordinary setup/remove never rewrite foreign connection definitions, copy private keys, weaken host-key policy, or treat every alias as a fleet member. Explicit format/organize may transform selected user-owned configuration with private guarded recovery; Include restores its caller scope after each file. Named agent providers (Bitwarden, 1Password, Secretive, custom sockets) are located by stat only and never executed; selecting a named-agent key publishes only its public line and writes a v2 fragment (`IdentityAgent`, `SecurityKeyProvider`), which older binaries treat as not dev-owned, while v1 files stay byte-identical. Explicit FIDO generation binds the reviewed native tools/provider, keeps capability observations stat-only, and reports hardware created/unknown effects independently of local publication; only verified SK recovery pairs may be retained. Never use resident-key download or provider loading as a passive probe, and keep automatic Secure Enclave creation blocked until exact native identity mapping is verified.
73	- `sshflow` owns the explicit SSH/fleet/Herdr machine inventory and Plan/Apply orchestration; `herdrremote` calls the native machine CLI without writing its catalog. `configedit` owns source-bound local file transactions and private recovery outside Git, with owner leases and macOS/Linux metadata checks.
74	- `machineregistry` owns controller-local canonical machine UUIDs, scoped provider bindings, explicit unlink suppression and merge redirects in durable private SQLite. 75	- `sshactivity` owns private durable per-profile usage and test observations. Usage records actual local dev-mediated SSH process starts; network/full tests never update usage. Observations retain source fingerprints and cannot authorize mutations or imply present connectivity.
76	- `tuiissue` owns typed problem guidance and reviewed native dependency installation recipes. UI actions use finite IDs and exact guarded service callbacks, never executable error text.
77	- `selfupdate` selects exact release platform assets and stages native Go source builds when an asset is absent, preferring the checksummed compact source archive over legacy Go module source. CLI owns confirmation and executable replacement; download/checksum failures never authorize a source fallback, and failed builds retain the installed binary.
78	- `platformfs` owns the native Android Termux home anchor, inherited app-data SELinux/encryption metadata recognition and no-replace publication. Verify the exact system/app prefix and all user-controlled descendants; never trust arbitrary UID-1000 directories, relabel files, chmod Android system paths or substitute an overwriting rename.

It never imports existing private keys or writes new private material to files. Experimental Bitwarden memory creation and delegation to a native profile need separate approvals; freeze the actual environment/cwd and revalidate session/profile/tool identity without exposing session values or hashes. A session or base URL is not endpoint identity: native-context consistency and endpoint-unverified status remain separate from creation and agent visibility. Native no-interaction must prevent private JSON stdin from becoming a credential response; ambiguous writes retain receipts and never auto-retry/delete. 87	
88	State is split intentionally:
89	
90	- Git remotes/branches are durable code truth.
91	- Worktrees are disposable local checkouts.
92	- Runtime sessions are per-host and re-derivable.
93	- Task TOML and catalog assets hold only intent/identity that Git cannot answer.
94	- Repository quick-note Markdown is durable sidecar data; `notes.db` is only its disposable search index.
95	- `stats.db` is durable observation data; `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev/*` is disposable.
96	- SSH source/route caches are disposable; remote dev UUIDs, local canonical machine UUIDs and fleet trust pins are separate identities. 97	- The user's OpenSSH configuration is durable connection truth. Plain `dev ssh list` stays static; `--tailscale` explicitly queries the optional local CLI and `--lan` reads cached observations. Neither list nor dashboard refresh scans the LAN. The active SSH dashboard may refresh local Tailscale status when `[tui.ssh].background_refresh` is enabled; native discovery returns typed observations independently of cache writes. Candidate setup preserves source/scope provenance and per-stage retained effects.
100	
101	## Behavioral contracts
102	
103	- Task modes are `worktree`, `branch`, and `direct`; lifecycle states are `hot`, `warm`, `cold`, and `done`. READY/REVIEW/MERGED/RETIRED are action readiness or result milestones, never extra persisted states.
104	- Persisted intent, observed facts, and guarded action plans are separate layers. Unknown, failed, skipped, loading, or stale observations never become a false clean/closed fact.
105	- Use an explicit base for branch/worktree creation. Do not infer a safe base from whichever branch happens to be checked out.
106	- Never nest a managed worktree inside a repository. Removing a worktree does not remove its branch, and dirty removal stays opt-in.
107	- Cold parking requires committed, pushed, reconstructible work before runtime/worktree cleanup.
108	- Submodule initialization uses committed gitlinks, never implicitly advances to `main`. Whole child-clone disposal requires explicit recursive approval and fresh recovery proof for its private refs/objects; outer and shared canonical repositories are retained. Local graph refresh never performs remote proof. Child task/runtime/artifact claims block parent disposal.
109	- A taskflow Plan is bound to the exact task revision and repository/worktree/ref/runtime/artifact identities shown at Plan time. Apply must lock, reload, and revalidate those identities; a changed revision or authority produces a stale-plan result with no new effect.
110	- Managed rows receive only legal mode/state lifecycle actions. An unmanaged linked checkout may be adopted by metadata-only task creation or removed only when exact, clean, unclaimed, non-harness, and branch-preserving; canonical, harness-owned, ambiguous/conflicting, locked, prunable, or incompletely observed rows fail closed for destructive actions.
111	- Local repository refresh must not contact remotes. Fetching refs and querying a forge are explicit network actions, and review evidence is run-local manual evidence limited to portable existence/state/draft/URL/provider/time fields; never infer review decisions or checks.
112	- Reconciliation flows such as `sweep`, command-level `adopt`, and bootstrap organization plans report before applying changes. Direct actions such as `wt rm`, `tries archive`, and `cache clear` mutate immediately after their own safety checks; do not treat them as previews. `dev flow` is plan-first regardless of the adapted command's normal CLI interaction.
113	- Raw Git and configured external tools remain outside dev-mediated locks, revalidation, and safety guarantees. Existing expert CLI flags remain compatibility surface even when the preview flow deliberately omits them.
114	- A recognized agent in a canonical checkout occupies it regardless of whether its status is working, idle, done, or unknown. Shared-writer overrides require coordinated disjoint ownership.
115	- A parallel launch target is only the exact root pane returned for a newly created first-class Herdr worktree; reused/fallback/unverified surfaces fail closed.
116	- `dev ls --json` is an external automation contract. Add fields rather than renaming/removing existing fields; apply the same compatibility care to other documented structured output, including `dev hygiene report --json` (`hygiene_summary` schema 1). Stored summaries are historical observations, not proof of current source bytes.
117	- Quick notes attach to the canonical repository through catalog identity. Markdown is durable, note deletion requires confirmation, and clearing/rebuilding note FTS must never delete source files.
118	- Explicit SSH format/organize and fleet profile rename/remove are plan-first exceptions for user-selected files; retain comments, Include order, original metadata and private recovery. Never activate dormant files with a new broad Include. Herdr machine add may prepare/start a remote server; leave native approvals native, and remove/disable never stops remote sessions.
119	- SSH initialization is report-before-apply; managed host changes are confined to canonical dev-owned fragments. Full bootstrap requires an explicit existing key or explicit generation, registers fleet only when explicitly selected, and reports interrupted remote installation as unknown rather than pretending to roll it back.
120	- SSH wizard permission preflight may separately review and apply metadata-only tightening on exact current-user-owned canonical/selected paths. It never recursively chmods, changes ownership, guesses ACLs, or widens permissions; completed repairs survive later cancellation. Listing and dry-run never repair permissions. Local key listing evaluates OpenSSH only behind explicit `--alias`; selected key material remains service-bound and is revalidated before configuration changes and bootstrap.
121	- `dev ssh key doctor` exposes the same permission Plan/Apply with bounded metadata-only key discovery; `--key` restricts the reviewed scope, and `--fix` requires a complete safe plan plus confirmation. Default doctor never mutates, reads private contents, or queries agents/remotes. Batch repairs revalidate the whole reviewed union and retain successful tightening on partial failure.
122	- Source-aware SSH setup can use `--auth existing` without installing a key, and registers only explicitly selected `--to fleet|herdr|both` destinations. Tailscale SSH advertisement is advisory; its port-22 endpoint is not an authorized_keys bootstrap target. Preserve the key-authentication guard and never treat Tailscale policy login as proof that a selected public key worked. Names, ports and cached observations never authorize machine merges; binding/source changes invalidate reviewed plans.
123	- Fleet-source SSH discovery selects explicit hosts without recursive fleet traversal. Local ProxyJump imports never copy remote identity/agent/trust paths; cached route data cannot authorize apply. `connect --on` is one interactive fixed-helper session with no agent forwarding or arbitrary command payload. Normal SSH errors retain child exit status.
124	- Controller password brokerage uses a private per-operation Unix socket or protected Windows pipe, never password argv/environment/files. Exact host/user/port/route contexts gate replies and save evidence. Remote source-to-target credentials remain outside this feature; native key/passphrase interaction is separate.
125	- Filesystem transitions must retain path traversal/symlink, same-filesystem, source revalidation, and rollback/reconciliation checks.
126	
127	## Versioning and changelog
128	
129	The current published baseline is `v0.2.39` (2026-09-17). The CLI version authority is an immutable `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` Git tag:
130	
131	- `Makefile` derives development builds with `git describe --tags --match 'v[0-9]*' --always --dirty` and injects `internal/cli.Version` through `-ldflags`. The `--match` filter is load-bearing: any other tag in the repository (a `backup/` or `rescue/` marker, say) must never become `--version`.
132	- `go install ...@version` recovers the module version from Go build information.
133	- `pyproject.toml` version `0.0.0` belongs only to the MkDocs environment and is not the CLI version.
134	
135	Every user-visible feature must be added to `[Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` as part of the feature change. Do not publish or describe a feature build under an older release's version; a release containing new compatible behavior must receive a newer version. Decide from public compatibility impact rather than blindly from the commit type.
136	
137	**When to release.** A tag is not an occasional ceremony; it is how a downstream binary learns it is stale. `go install ...@latest` resolves to the newest tag, so anything merged but untagged is invisible outside this repository.
138	
139	- A landed branch that stands alone is released immediately: bump the patch during `0.x` (`v0.1.x`) and tag it as the last step of landing.
140	- A landed branch belonging to an announced milestone accumulates in `[Unreleased]`; the milestone closes with a minor bump (`v0.2.0`).
141	- Never let `[Unreleased]` grow past one milestone's worth of work. `v0.1.0` to `v0.1.11` were tagged retroactively on 2026-08-29 precisely because 38 commits accumulated with no release.
142	
143	**What downstream gets.** Every release from `v0.2.0` forward publishes platform binaries and `SHA256SUMS` alongside the GitHub release, and `dev doctor` reports the running version so a user can compare without leaving the terminal. A release that ships neither leaves `dev --version` as the only signal, which is what the freshness work exists to fix.
144	
145	For a release:
146	
147	1. Move the relevant `[Unreleased]` entries into `## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD` and update comparison links.
148	2. Update version-pinned install examples when the documented recommended release changes.
149	3. Push `main` first. `release.yml` asserts the tagged commit is an ancestor of `origin/main`, so a tag pushed ahead of its branch fails validation.
150	4. Tag the exact commit on `main` as `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`; never move or reuse a published tag. Never push `backup/*` or `rescue/*` tags — a tag reachable from a commit that predates the `--match` filter breaks the workflow's `./dev --version` assertion.
151	5. Let `.github/workflows/release.yml` run CI, verify `./dev --version`, build the platform matrix, create the GitHub release, and publish the matching Homebrew formula. The repository secret `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` must be a fine-grained token with Contents write access to `daviddwlee84/homebrew-tap`; a tap publication failure fails the release job so it can be retried instead of leaving Homebrew users stale.
152	
153	If the Homebrew step needs a retry or an older stable release needs a one-time backfill, run `gh workflow run publish-homebrew.yml -f version=vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. The manual workflow verifies that the release exists and republishes only the formula; it does not create or move a tag or GitHub release.
154	
155	Stable release tags only are accepted by the current workflow; prerelease tags are not supported.
156	
157	## Keep implementation, skill, and docs aligned
158	
159	`internal/skill/dev-cli/` is shipped product surface, not incidental prose: `internal/skill/skill.go` embeds the entire tree in the binary. A code change is incomplete when the bundled skill or public documentation still describes old behavior.
160	
161	| Change | Required synchronization |
162	|---|---|
163	| Cobra command name, `Use`, `Short`, flag, or global option | Run `make skill-sync`, inspect `internal/skill/dev-cli/references/commands.md`, then run `make skill-check`. Never edit the generated block by hand. |
164	| Task modes/states/defaults or lifecycle preconditions | Update `SKILL.md`, `references/task-lifecycle.md`, README, embedded help, relevant English and zh-TW workflow/mental-model/compatibility pages, and transition tests. |
165	| Worktree placement, provisioning, include rules, strategies, or safety checks | Update `references/worktree-ownership.md`, README/public worktree docs, config examples, and focused `wt` tests. |
166	| Runtime protocol, fallback order, activation, agent collision, exact-pane launch, or cleanup behavior | Update `references/runtime-herdr.md`, `references/parallel-agents.md`, compatibility docs, and runtime/lifecycle tests. Keep the boundary clear: `dev start` prepares a checkout/runtime surface; it does not launch an agent. |
167	| Bootstrap scan/layout/index/move behavior | Update `references/bootstrap.md`, public bootstrap docs, and bootstrap tests. |
168	| Config fields/defaults or structured output | Update generated command help where applicable, authored reference pages and both locales, examples, and compatibility tests. |
169	| Quick-note storage, identity, search, structured output, or TUI behavior | Update README, embedded help, `SKILL.md`, `references/notes.md`, and paired English/zh-TW mental-model, workflow, TUI, commands/config, compatibility, and freshness pages. |
170	| Any user-visible feature or fix | Update `CHANGELOG.md`; update README/help/MkDocs/skill wherever they make the affected claim. |
171	
172	`make skill-check` proves only that generated command syntax matches the Cobra tree. It cannot detect drift in lifecycle semantics, JSON schemas, safety claims, examples, README, embedded help, or authored skill references; review those manually. Because the skill is compiled with `go:embed`, rebuild after any skill edit before testing the bundled output.
173	
174	English and zh-TW MkDocs pages are maintained as a pair. Run the strict documentation checks above after changing either locale, navigation, snippets, or freshness metadata.

177	
178	`internal/hygiene` owns per-repository setup plans and batch ledgers. REPOS and

180	artifact finalizers until their independent lifecycle is replaced. Cached machine

188	
189	`dev help ai-artifacts` separates source retention, archive location, protection
190	and distribution. New configuration is opt-in. Sources are SpecStory Markdown or
191	explicit files; provider IDs name the originating agent. Do not infer writer exit

235	syntax and re-validates the file. If a `backlog/<slug>.md` exists for the
236	item, also mark it as shipped (don't delete — keep it as historical record).
237	
238	Keep `## Done` as the recent history buffer. Prune it into `CHANGELOG.md` only
239	when it contains items from a previous calendar year or grows past 20 entries.
240	
241	### External skill / MCP / domain / curiosity catalog -> `docs/catalog/`
242	
243	`docs/catalog/` is the vendoring decision log + external-awareness
244	registry, separate from `Skills` (what we ship) and `Reference` (our
245	own conventions). It has four subareas:
246	
247	- `docs/catalog/domains/` — per-domain hub pages (one per professional
248	  domain: Finance, Quant Research, AI/ML Research, Web & Fullstack,
249	  Knowledge Work, Agent Harness). Each hub aggregates local + vendored
250	  + external skills + MCPs relevant to that domain. New hubs copy
251	  [`docs/_snippets/domain-hub-template.md`](docs/_snippets/domain-hub-template.md).
252	- `docs/catalog/skill-collections.md` — single curated index of all
253	  upstream skill collections (Anthropic, Vercel, Supabase, marimo,
254	  Warp Oz, Orchestra-Research, etc.) with status per entry. Replaces
255	  the historical `Collections.md` (kept as a stub).
256	- `docs/catalog/curiosities.md` — docs-only shelf for interesting,
257	  provocative, or highly personal skills that are deliberately excluded
258	  from `vendor.yaml`, marketplace grouping, and routine skill discovery.
259	  Entries use `skipped` with the reason they remain docs-only.
260	- `docs/catalog/mcp/` — MCP wiki, modeled after Karpathy's
261	  [LLM Wiki pattern](docs/reference/llm-wiki-pattern.md). One markdown
262	  file per MCP with required YAML frontmatter
263	  (`name / slug / upstream_url / transport / auth / hosting / domain /
264	  status / license / last_verified`).
265	
266	Every external entry carries a status enum (single source of truth in
267	`docs/_snippets/external-install.md`):
268	
269	| Status | Meaning |
270	|---|---|
271	| `vendored` | In `vendor.yaml` — link to the entry. |
272	| `deferred` | Open `TODO P?` item — link to it. |
273	| `skipped` | Looked at, chose not to vendor — inline reason required. |
274	| `evaluated` | Read but no decision — 1-line note. |
275	| `wishlist` | Surfaced but not yet evaluated — default for fresh discoveries. |
276	
277	Status changes trigger existing scripts:
278	`wishlist → deferred` runs `add-todo.sh`; `deferred → vendored` runs
279	`add-vendor.sh` + optionally `promote-todo.sh`. Full recipe in
280	[`docs/workflows/adding-catalog-entries.md`](docs/workflows/adding-catalog-entries.md).
281	
282	Every published catalog page is bilingual (`*.md` + `*.zh-TW.md`).
283	Snippets and `_template.md` are EN-only by convention.
284	
285	### Past pitfalls -> `pitfalls/`
286	
287	When a debugging session uncovers a non-obvious trap that could realistically be
288	hit again, write `pitfalls/<slug>.md` with:
289	
290	1. The verbatim symptom or error text
291	2. The root cause
292	3. The workaround
293	4. Prevention guidance or the hard invariant that supersedes it
294	
295	Use symptom-first titles so future agents can grep the failure they see, not
296	the explanation they do not know yet.

# Agent history hygiene

Preserve selected agent evidence under the repository's chosen policy. Read
`dev help ai-artifacts` and `dev artifact status` when supported: source tracking,
external archive, protection and distribution are separate choices. Commit
reviewed project knowledge; do not force-add raw history under archive/unmanaged
policy. Verify repository protection from the effective hook chain.

## Prefer the shared dev workflow

When the installed dev supports `hygiene`, use its domain for setup, scans,
private rules and reviewed text changes:

```bash
dev hygiene status
dev hygiene setup --json
dev hygiene setup --apply --plan <id> --yes
dev hygiene scan --scope staged --json
dev hygiene scan --scope history --audit --timeout 40m --json
```

`pre-commit` and `gitleaks` are needed for this repository hook recipe. An explicitly unscanned archive copy needs neither. A global `core.hooksPath` can be
correct, but its script may skip all checks when repository configs are absent.
The shared setup preserves existing hooks/comments and refuses an unverified
chain. Repository new/setup's `agent-history-hygiene` initializer uses this same
service. New default hooks block; they do not rewrite or stage files.

Per-repo secret/known/generic policy supports block/warn/off, with private local
overrides and exact reasoned exceptions. Private visibility is advice, never an
automatic exemption. SSH imports are static and reviewed: no DNS, login, Match
exec, private-key reads or rule-value export. Personal rules stay outside Git;
CI checks public rules and must state the missing personal coverage.

Read the bundled dev reference `references/hygiene.md` through `dev help hygiene`
or the public hygiene guide before rule changes or redaction. The CLI supports
all regular text, rather than treating transcripts as the only leak surface.

## Preserve the review trail

1. Identify the exact provider/session UUID from the transcript preamble. Never
   select another session just because its file is newest.
2. Commit product changes and reviewed plans. Follow the selected retention
   policy for raw history; do not broadly stage every agent directory.
3. Use `dev prepare --session provider:uuid` and finalization after its writer
   exits when that lifecycle applies. Byte stability alone is not writer proof.
4. Scan exact staged content. Partial staging must not accidentally stage
   unrelated working-copy edits.
5. In archive mode, raw history may be ignored but must be preserved before
   checkout disposal. In track mode, retain the existing exact-session workflow.
   Exclude conversation evidence from product source archives independently.

Do not close, restart or spawn agents to make hygiene checks pass without the
applicable authorization. A new agent without SpecStory does not stop an older
writer. Preserve the user's original task while offering additional cleanup.

## Reviewed redaction

```bash
dev hygiene redact --report <report-id> --file <reviewed-file> --json
# After reviewing, and after the exact artifact writer exited:
dev hygiene redact --apply --plan <plan-id> --yes --writer-stopped
```

Plans bind native file identity, contents, policy and checkout state. Stale,
modified or partial plans are not authority to overwrite current data. Keep
private recovery and rerun scans/tests after source or configuration changes.
The running transcript is left for a manual external trigger after its writer
stops. No automatic history rewrite, agent launch, commit, push or cleanup occurs.

## External archive workflow

`dev artifact setup` and `dev repo setup --artifacts` preview explicit per-repo
policy. `archive --session provider:uuid` or `--file` creates reviewed snapshots;
apply only after the exact recorder exits. Off/check/redact affect the copy,
not the live source or its index. A disabled scan is recorded as skipped.
Checked snapshots produce masked finding IDs for reasoned fixture exceptions.

Commit reviewed plans with product work before `dev prepare`. New archive intents
bind the destination and policy; redact finalization requires a reviewed
`--archive-plan`. Old tracked intents retain the compatibility scripts below.
Keep those installations while any tracked workflow still depends on them.

`artifact find` reads local committed archive records. Sync and original-backup
publication are explicit Git operations; they never transfer native session DBs.
`artifact migrate` can untrack after verified backup or build separate original,
history and filtered Git copies with commit maps. It never force-pushes source
refs. For historical exposure, use the remediation section rather than treating
path removal as a secret audit. Private raw recovery is not cache.

## Legacy scripts

The scripts remain explicit compatibility utilities. Prefer dev for new setup
and partial-staging-safe edits; a separately published remote redactor hook has
its own version and is not silently updated by dev.

- `find-session.sh --json`: locate candidate transcript/plan metadata.
- `stage-agent-artifacts.sh --session-only --dry-run`: inspect exact staging;
  without session-only it may include other dirty artifacts, so use cautiously.
- `scan-staged.sh`: masked JSON-lines locations only, never raw Match/Secret.
  Exit 0 means clean; 20 means candidate findings; legacy `--redact` selects
  exit 10 but only masks output, never modifies files. Exit 30 means missing
  gitleaks; 40 means scanner/JSON/required-parser failure; 2 means not in Git.
- `assets/redact_secrets.py --fix`: explicit legacy artifact mutation. Scanner
  failure is an error, not an empty result; console output uses full sentinels.
  This utility can restage, so use the reviewed dev flow for partial staging.
- `bootstrap-project.sh`: legacy installer; new default templates require dev
  hygiene. Its old `--migrate` targets the separately published remote redactor,
  not the new dev policy migration. Prefer `dev hygiene setup`.

SpecStory may already redact on write, but provider behavior/version is not proof
that every secret class or artifact directory is covered. Preserve existing
`[REDACTED:<rule-id>]` markers. An inert marker must never exempt another secret
on the same line. `.gitleaksignore` contains exact finding fingerprints, not
file/path globs. Portable pattern exceptions need a narrow rule/path/match scope.

## Confirmed historical exposures

Read [remediation](references/remediation.md). First distinguish fixtures,
examples and scanner candidates from confirmed credentials. Revoke/rotate a
confirmed exposed credential at its provider before considering Git history.

Shared main and immutable release tags stay unchanged in ordinary hygiene work.
Correct HEAD in a new commit, and assess old commits, tags, PR references, forks,
clones, caches and distribution artifacts separately. A force push does not erase
all copies or revoke a credential. Personal names, Git author metadata and filenames
also need an explicit impact assessment; text replacement does not rewrite them.

Never echo matching bytes or raw process arguments into a chat to investigate a
finding. Use rule IDs, safe locations and private local reports. Keep raw reports,
recovery images and personal identity dictionaries outside Git and CI logs.

## Validation

Run the skill's fixture tests for redactor/scan-wrapper changes. For dev changes,
run native hygiene/storage/text-transaction tests and the real hook test:

```bash
python scripts/test-hygiene-hooks.py --dev <absolute-built-dev>
```

It uses an isolated HOME/repository and synthetic credentials. Validate same-line
placeholder bypasses, hidden files, partial staging, missing/malformed scanner
results, writer/stale-plan refusal and private recovery. Synchronize embedded
bootstrap assets and both locales of public documentation.

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
herdr machine
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` and `done` both mean the agent is ready for input. The CLI/API uses the server's seen state to distinguish them; explicit focus commands mark the target seen, while reads do not. Each TUI client tracks viewed completions independently, so its Done badge can differ from the CLI or another client's badge. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

IDs and live agent names are scoped to one server. Two saved SSH machines can both have `w1:p1` or an agent named `reviewer`. Selecting a machine in the TUI does not retarget commands running in your pane: they still use the inherited session and socket context. Run remote control commands on the intended host with its explicit session, and rediscover IDs there.

`herdr machine list` lists saved connection profiles, not a cross-machine pane inventory; add `--json` for scripts. Only add, remove, enable, or disable profiles when the user asks. Removing a profile disconnects the client but does not stop remote sessions. Adding a machine uses the remote default session unless `--remote-session` is explicitly supplied. Setup asks before stopping an incompatible server and defaults to No; do not approve replacement without the user's consent. Experimental handoff is not part of `machine add`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter as one ordered submission. It reports successful submission only after both have been written; that alone does not prove the agent started a turn. The submit delay grows with prompt size for Codex on Windows. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

With `--wait`, a prompt sent from a non-working state must produce observed `working` or `blocked` activity. After submission, Herdr waits up to five seconds for that activity; unrelated `idle`, `done`, or session changes do not satisfy this gate. It returns `agent_prompt_stalled` if no activity is observed, or `timeout` if the caller's timeout expires first. The caller timeout includes submission time. Without a timeout, the settled-state wait is indefinite after activity is observed. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. A timeout or stalled response does not prove the prompt was never delivered; do not blindly submit it again. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked. `workspace close --group` closes the primary workspace and its linked worktree workspaces; never add it merely to bypass `workspace_group_close_required`.
- Use `--trust-repository` only after the user has verified the repository. It grants per-request Git trust; it is not a routine retry for a failed worktree command.
- Client and server versions can differ after an update. Check `herdr status` before relying on new server features. A missing method is not permission to stop or upgrade a server.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

389	// OpenWorktree implements WorktreeOpener: it registers an already-created git
390	// worktree as a herdr workspace, which is what makes the checkout appear in
391	// the sidebar grouped under its parent repo with its own branch and
392	// ahead/behind row.
393	func (h *Herdr) OpenWorktree(ctx context.Context, path, label string) (OpenResult, error) {
394		args := []string{"worktree", "open"}
395		if source := h.parentWorktreeSource(ctx, path); source != "" {
396			// Pin the canonical parent checkout instead of relying on the calling
397			// pane. This preserves native nested grouping even when dev is invoked
398			// from a different Herdr workspace.
399			args = append(args, "--cwd", source)
400		} else if h.session != "" {
401			return OpenResult{}, errors.New("cannot resolve an explicit parent checkout for scoped Herdr preparation")
402		}
403		args = append(args, "--path", path, "--no-focus")
404		if label != "" {
405			args = append(args, "--label", label)
406		}
407		var res struct {
408			Workspace   herdrWorkspace `json:"workspace"`
409			Worktree    herdrWorktree  `json:"worktree"`
410			RootPane    herdrPane      `json:"root_pane"`
411			AlreadyOpen *bool          `json:"already_open"`
412		}
413		if err := h.call(ctx, &res, args...); err != nil {
414			if h.session != "" {
415				return OpenResult{}, fmt.Errorf("scoped Herdr worktree open failed; any partial workspace is retained for inspection: %w", err)
416			}
417			// Fall back to a plain workspace: the checkout being visible matters
418			// more than it being tagged with git provenance. A fallback root pane is
419			// withheld so callers cannot mistake it for a first-class worktree target.
420			fallback, fallbackErr := h.Open(ctx, path, label)
421			fallback.RootPaneID = ""
422			fallback.Surface = "workspace"
423			return fallback, fallbackErr
424		}
425		handle := res.Workspace.WorkspaceID
426		if handle == "" {
427			handle = res.Worktree.OpenWorkspaceID
428		}
429		if handle == "" {
430			return OpenResult{}, fmt.Errorf("herdr worktree open: response has no workspace id")
431		}
432		if res.AlreadyOpen == nil {
433			// Without this protocol field, the handle may belong to a reused
434			// workspace. Do not close it or expose its pane as newly created.
435			return OpenResult{}, fmt.Errorf("herdr worktree open: response does not say whether the workspace was reused")
436		}
437		created := !*res.AlreadyOpen
438		if created && (res.RootPane.PaneID == "" || res.RootPane.WorkspaceID != handle) {
439			return OpenResult{}, h.rejectCreatedWorkspace(ctx, handle,
440				"herdr worktree open: new workspace response has no correlated root pane")
441		}
442		rootPaneID := ""
443		if created {
444			rootPaneID = res.RootPane.PaneID
445		}
446		return OpenResult{
447			Handle: handle, Surface: "worktree", Opened: true,
448			Created: created, RootPaneID: rootPaneID,
449		}, nil
450	}
451	
452	func (h *Herdr) rejectCreatedWorkspace(ctx context.Context, handle, reason string) error {
453		if h.session != "" {
454			return fmt.Errorf("%s; retained incomplete workspace %s in Herdr session %s for inspection", reason, handle, h.session)
455		}
456		if err := h.Close(ctx, handle); err != nil {
457			return fmt.Errorf("%s; could not close incomplete workspace %s: %w", reason, handle, err)
458		}
459		return fmt.Errorf("%s; closed incomplete workspace %s", reason, handle)
460	}
461	
462	func (h *Herdr) parentWorktreeSource(ctx context.Context, path string) string {
463		if h.worktreeSource != nil {
464			return h.worktreeSource(ctx, path)
465		}
466		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "-C", path, "worktree", "list", "--porcelain")
467		out, err := cmd.Output()
468		if err != nil {
469			return ""
470		}
471		var parent string
472		for _, line := range strings.Split(string(out), "\n") {
473			switch {
474			case strings.HasPrefix(line, "worktree ") && parent == "":
475				parent = strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "worktree "))
476			case line == "" && parent != "":
477				if info, err := os.Stat(parent); err == nil && info.IsDir() {
478					return filepath.Clean(parent)
479				}
480				return ""
481			}
482		}
483		return ""
484	}
485	
486	// Close implements Runtime. This ends herdr's session state only — it never
487	// removes the checkout, the worktree or the branch, matching herdr's own
488	// separation of `workspace close` from `worktree remove`.
489	func (h *Herdr) Close(ctx context.Context, handle string) error {
490		if handle == "" {
491			return nil
492		}
493		return h.call(ctx, nil, "workspace", "close", handle)
494	}
495	
496	// Annotate implements Runtime by reporting display-only workspace metadata.
497	//
498	// Note for users: a token only renders if the sidebar row layout in
499	// ~/.config/herdr/config.toml names it, e.g. rows = [[..., "$stage"], ["$next"]].
500	// Setting a token with no matching layout entry succeeds silently and shows
501	// nothing.
502	func (h *Herdr) Annotate(ctx context.Context, handle string, kv map[string]string) error {
503		if handle == "" || len(kv) == 0 {
504			return nil
505		}
506		args := []string{"workspace", "report-metadata", handle, "--source", h.metadataSource}
507		for k, v := range kv {
508			if v == "" {
509				args = append(args, "--clear-token", k)
510				continue
511			}
512			args = append(args, "--token", k+"="+v)
513		}
514		return h.call(ctx, nil, args...)
515	}
516	
517	func keys(m map[string]bool) []string {
518		if len(m) == 0 {
519			return nil
520		}
521		out := make([]string, 0, len(m))
522		for k := range m {
523			out = append(out, k)
524		}
525		for i := 1; i < len(out); i++ {
526			for j := i; j > 0 && out[j] < out[j-1]; j-- {
527				out[j], out[j-1] = out[j-1], out[j]
528			}
529		}
530		return out
531	}

6	# dev-cli
7	
8	Git owns durable code; worktrees are local checkouts; runtimes are host-local
9	sessions; dev records task intent.
10	
11	## Discover what you need
12	
13	Use `dev <command> --help` for current syntax and flags, and `dev help <topic>`
14	for workflow explanations. `dev --help` lists commands; `dev help` lists topics.
15	Prefer supported `--json` output for automation. Read the relevant command before
16	mutation: some actions execute immediately, while others require preview/apply.
17	Do not preload manuals, repeat `dev --skill`, or run routine diagnostics.
18	
19	## Preserve these boundaries
20	
21	- Opening a repository needs no task. Choose direct, branch, or worktree
22	  deliberately; pass an explicit `--base` for branch/worktree creation. Keep
23	  managed worktrees outside repositories.
24	- `dev start` normally prepares a checkout/runtime. Agent launch is explicit.
25	  Parallel writers need coordinated ownership and verified launch targets.
26	- Completion, artifact finalization, retirement and branch deletion are separate.
27	  Finalize after writer exit; retire externally. Use `retire --base` when a fork
28	  point cannot prove integration. Runtime `done` is not cleanup-ready.
29	- Unknown or cached observations, merged PRs, and command refusals do not grant
30	  cleanup authority. Resolve the reported conditions; do not improvise force
31	  removal or bypass trust checks.

1	# Worktree ownership
2	
3	Submodule initialization is core Git acquisition, before provisioning/runtime, and defaults to recursive pinned checkouts. `--no-provision` does not skip it; `--submodules=none` does. Gitlink children are independent submodule clones, not nested managed linked worktrees. Read `submodules.md` for selection and explicit disposal rules.
4	
5	Read this before creating a worktree, sharing a checkout between agents, or when
6	a new checkout lacks dependencies, env files, or launcher backend state.
7	
8	## The rule
9	
10	| Change boundary | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
11	|---|---|---|---|
12	| Durable feature/fix/experiment/handoff | **`dev`** | `paths.worktree_path` | until external `dev retire` |
13	| Harness-owned turn-scoped isolation | Claude Code | `.claude/worktrees/` | managed by that harness; do not assume artifact relocation |
14	| Runtime workspace/panes | Herdr | per-host runtime | until explicitly closed |
15	| Rendered agent history | SpecStory | process launch checkout | until committed/removed with that checkout |
16	
17	Use a `dev` worktree for independent approaches or any change stream whose code,
18	history, or plan must remain reviewable. Agents with explicitly disjoint file
19	ownership may share one checkout, but `--allow-shared-checkout` is a deliberate
20	coordination override—not a default.
21	
22	`EnterWorktree` changes an agent's working location; it does not prove an
23	existing SpecStory wrapper/watcher rebound its source/output paths. Start the
24	new process from the target worktree root.
25	
26	## Why dev creates the checkout
27	
28	`dev` runs `git worktree add`, then asks Herdr to run
29	`worktree open --path <path> --no-focus`. Path policy therefore remains stable
30	on machines without Herdr, while Herdr still displays repo/branch provenance.
31	A fallback plain workspace is reported as such and is not an exact agent launch
32	target.
33	
34	Never nest a durable worktree inside another checkout. Every watcher, language
35	server, backup tool and search then sees a second copy of the repository.
36	
37	Herdr's native **New worktree** action is still valid for an external,
38	unmanaged checkout. When the canonical repository is under a configured scan
39	root, Git registration lets dev discover the checkout without scanning
40	`~/.herdr/worktrees`; dev does not auto-adopt, relocate, or provision it. Run
41	`dev wt provision <path>` if it needs the project environment and `dev adopt`
42	followed by `dev adopt --apply` only when it should enter the durable task
43	lifecycle. For one exact checkout, `dev flow [repo]` offers plan-first
44	metadata-only Adopt and clean branch-preserving Remove Checkout. It never removes
45	the canonical checkout or a harness/conflicting/locked/prunable/task-claimed row,
46	and it does not prune repository-wide stale registrations.
47	
48	## Paths
49	
50	Default:
51	
52	```text
53	~/Worktrees/<repo>/<branch-slug>
54	```
55	
56	Configurable through `paths.worktree_root` and `paths.worktree_path`, with
57	`worktree_root`, `repo`, `repo_path`, `branch`, `category`, `host`, and `date`
58	variables plus `slug`, `lower`, and `base` filters.
59	
60	Always pass `--base` for unattended creation so the intended starting point is
61	explicit. `dev start` and `dev wt create` otherwise resolve the repository's
62	default branch; they do not use whichever feature happens to be checked out.
63	
64	## Provisioning
65	
66	A worktree is a clean checkout. `dev wt create` and `dev start` build and apply
67	an inspectable plan:
68	
69	```bash
70	dev wt plan
71	dev wt plan --write
72	dev wt provision --dry-run
73	```
74	
75	Effective settings come from global config or committed repo
76	`.dev-cli/config.toml` (legacy `.dev.toml` remains readable):
77	
78	```toml
79	[worktree]
80	include = [".env", ".env.local"]
81	link = []
82	post_create = "auto"
83	strategy = "reinstall"
84	```
85	
86	An executable `post_create` from `.dev-cli/config.toml` requires approval of its
87	exact content hash with `dev config trust <repo> --yes`. Legacy `.dev.toml`
88	retains its compatibility behavior.
89	
90	Only paths that are both explicitly included and genuinely gitignored are
91	copied. Tracked files already have the branch-correct version. Included files
92	must remain the same regular file from validation through open; source swaps and
93	symlinked destination parents are refused. Existing destinations are reported
94	as skipped, never falsely as copied, and file contents are never logged.
95	
96	This is local provisioning only. Off-machine `dev fleet files` deliberately uses
97	a separate `[local_files].include` allowlist plus explicit `--to`; never infer
98	export permission from `[worktree].include`.
99	
100	### Project-local Claude backend state
101	
102	`.claude/settings.local.json` stays gitignored and is **not** a universal default
103	include. The verified `claude-copilot-once` wrapper preserves an existing
104	Copilot pin and creates/removes only its own pin when one was absent;
105	`codex-copilot-once` injects its backend via CLI. Neither needs a copied project
106	file. Claude's Copilot proxy must already be running; the Codex path may
107	self-start its proxy flow.
108	
109	An explicitly selected sticky/plain-Claude profile may opt in exactly:
110	
111	```toml
112	[worktree]
113	include = [".env", ".env.local", ".claude/settings.local.json"]
114	```
115	
116	Verify the file arrived before launch. If absent, stop instead of allowing the
117	launcher to fall back silently to another backend. `dev` logs the relative path
118	only, never its contents.
119	
120	## Dependency strategies
121	
122	- `reinstall`: safe default; run lockfile-derived installer.
123	- `copy`: duplicate path-independent dependency trees.
124	- `link`: explicit and usually unsafe for mutable dependencies.
125	- `skip`: for external/container-managed environments.
126	
127	`dev` refuses unsound choices, such as copied/linked Python virtualenvs, and
128	reports missing tools or failed setup without deleting the usable checkout.
129	
130	## Cleanup
131	
132	- `dev wt rm <branch>` removes only the checkout after external runtime safety checks; branch survives.
133	- `dev park` records WARM; when called from its own runtime it leaves that runtime alive for normal exit.
134	- `dev park --cold --push` closes eligible runtime state and removes the pushed worktree only from outside.
135	- `dev done --ff` integrates and records MERGED; runtime/worktree/branch survive.
```

```text
1	# Worktrees
2	
3	Submodule workspaces initialize recursively at committed gitlinks by default.
4	Use `--submodules=none` to skip, or `start --submodule PATH` to select children
5	for task branches. `dev submodule status/init/develop/recover` inspects, prepares
6	and restores child checkouts. Explicit `--recursive` cleanup verifies initialized
7	child clones' remote recovery before removing them and the outer linked worktree;
8	canonical repositories and the outer branch are retained.
9	
10	A worktree is a second working directory for the same repository: its own
11	files, its own checked-out branch, sharing one history and one remote.
12	
13	## What they are actually for
14	
15	**Preventing two writers from editing the same files at once.** Not feature
16	management — that is what branches are for.
17	
18	So the question is never "how many agents am I running?" It is:
19	
20	> Could these two writers touch the same file?
21	
22	- Different files, one goal → one checkout is fine. Several agents, several
23	  panes, one branch.
24	- Different *approaches* to the same problem → one worktree each, so they can
25	  be compared and the loser discarded.
26	- Anything where the file ranges are unknown → worktrees.
27	
28	## Who owns which worktree
29	
30	| Kind | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
31	|---|---|---|---|
32	| Feature, fix, experiment, handoff | `dev` | `~/Worktrees/<repo>/<slug>` | until external retirement |
33	| Harness-owned turn-scoped isolation | Claude Code | `.claude/worktrees/` | owned by that harness; no transcript-relocation guarantee |
34	
35	**Might you review or return to the code/history/plan later → `dev`.**
36	
37	Never put a long-lived worktree inside the repository. Every file watcher,
38	language server, indexer and `rg` run in the outer repo then sees a second copy
39	of the whole tree.
40	
41	## Commands
42	
43	```bash
44	dev wt create feat/auth --base main   # create at the configured path
45	dev wt list                           # every worktree of this repo
46	dev wt open feat/auth                 # open an existing one
47	dev wt rm feat/auth                   # remove the checkout; branch survives
48	dev wt provision                      # re-run setup on an existing checkout
49	```
50	
51	## Always pass a base
52	
53	```bash
54	dev wt create fix/orderbook --base main
55	```
56	
57	Without `--base`, dev uses the repository's default branch. Passing it
58	explicitly is still preferred for scripts and agent-driven creation because
59	the intended committed starting point stays reviewable in the command.
60	
61	## Worktrees created directly in Herdr
62	
63	Herdr's **New worktree** action is allowed. Git registers that checkout with
64	the canonical repository, so dev can display it as an external worktree as
65	long as the canonical repo is discoverable through `paths.scan_roots` or
66	`paths.repo_paths`—even
67	when the checkout lives under `~/.herdr/worktrees` and that directory is not a
68	scan root.
69	
70	It remains deliberately unmanaged: dev does not silently create a task, move
71	the checkout, or run provisioning. If the work becomes durable, opt in:
72	
73	```bash
74	dev wt provision /path/to/worktree  # optional: env files + dependencies
75	dev adopt                           # report candidates; changes nothing
76	dev adopt --apply                   # record the selected candidates as tasks
77	```
78	
79	Until adoption, `dev park`, `dev resume`, and `dev done` have no task lifecycle
80	to operate on. Use `dev start` when that lifecycle is wanted from the outset.
81	
82	`dev flow [repo]` also shows every registered checkout. An eligible unmanaged
83	linked row offers plan-first **Adopt** (task metadata only; bytes stay untouched)
84	and **Remove Checkout** (clean, non-force, branch always preserved). Canonical,
85	harness, locked/prunable, task-claimed, or ambiguous rows have no destructive
86	path. Flow does not prune repository-wide stale registrations; inspect and repair
87	those explicitly.
88	
89	## A worktree starts empty of everything untracked
90	
91	No `node_modules`, no `.venv`, no `.env`. `dev` fixes this on create:
92	
93	- copies the gitignored files listed in `worktree.include`;
94	- symlinks anything in `worktree.link` (opt-in);
95	- runs `post_create`, detected from lockfiles when set to `"auto"`.
96	
97	Only files that are **both listed and gitignored** are copied. A tracked file
98	is already in the checkout on the correct branch — copying the other branch's
99	version over it would be wrong.
100	
101	## Removing one
102	
103	```bash
104	dev wt rm feat/auth
105	```
106	
107	Never deletes the branch. A dirty checkout needs an explicit `--force`, and
108	that refusal is the feature, not an obstacle.
109	
110	Gitlinks still need `--recursive`, even if never initialized. For linked-worktree
111	removal only, an absent or truly empty child path with no retained Git store may
112	be proved empty locally; no initialization, download, remote proof or push is
113	needed merely for removal. Retained/deinitialized data, orphan stores, local or
114	ignored files, unexpected `.git`, symlinks/reparse points, external claims and
115	incomplete observations block. Path-based task/artifact claims protect empty
116	children without inheriting parent Git identity; any non-discarded matching
117	artifact intent blocks, and discarded records still bind the reviewed authority.
118	
119	Physical emptiness alone is not removal permission. Manually deleting a tracked
120	gitlink directory makes the parent dirty, blocking ordinary non-force removal
121	before admin pruning. Cleanup never silently creates or restores placeholders to
122	bypass this guard. A never-initialized, Git-created empty directory can pass;
123	an absent child alone does not prove the parent safe to remove.
124	
125	Only exact reviewed empty modules admin scaffolding may be pruned under locks,
126	revalidating directory identity and emptiness immediately before native
127	directory-only removal. Empty checkout directories stay for normal non-force Git
128	removal. Real child stores retain full recovery proofs and journals/rollback;
129	partial pruning failure is not retirement success. Layout changes, new child
130	initialization or claims require a new plan. General removal guards and
131	initialization/publication policy are unchanged; no recursive file-deletion
132	workaround is used. See `dev help retirement` and `dev help ai-artifacts`.
133	
134	If a directory was deleted behind Git's back, the registration is a recovery
135	case. Inspect repository-wide `git worktree prune` scope before applying it;
136	`dev flow` reports the drift and does not prune implicitly.
137

17	go test ./internal/gitx -run '^TestAddWorktreeUsesExplicitBase$'  # one test
18	go test ./internal/cli -run '^TestName/Subtest$'                  # one subtest
19	make vet                           # go vet ./...
20	files="$(gofmt -l .)" && test -z "$files"  # format check that preserves gofmt failures
21	make e2e                           # real CLI lifecycle in an isolated temporary HOME
22	make skill-sync                    # regenerate command docs, then rebuild embedded skill
23	make skill-check                   # fail when command tree and generated skill reference drift
24	make install                       # binary under PREFIX; skill in user agent directories
25	```
26	
27	Documentation uses the same sequence as CI:
28	
29	```bash
30	uv sync --frozen --extra docs
31	uv run python scripts/check-docs.py --source
32	uv run mkdocs build --strict
33	uv run python scripts/check-docs.py --site site
34	```
35	
36	If generated `docs/llms*.txt` files drift, regenerate them with `uv run python scripts/check-docs.py --source --generate-llms` and then rerun the documentation checks.
